title: Contemplating Love Amid The Mists Of Grief; Tijuana Cure

contact_edits.before: The casting must be intended to provide a distancing effect, to avoid theobvious danger of self-exploitation. Up to a point it succeeds. Lucs, under Ashlie Corcoran's direction, makes no attempt to imitate Coleman, or indeed to do any kind of male impersonation at all. She's an actress with a strong physical and vocal presence that quite often goes into overdrive: I've never known so much juice to be squeezed from simple place-names. This wide-eyed over-emphasis, pervasive in the earlier parts of the evening, is the direct opposite of the discretion the play needs. It's the wrong kind of alienation. Later on, the performance settles down. A woman's body takes the curse off, while adding a comedic edge to, the narrator's rueful preoccupation with his own physicality. Lucs also of course gets to play all the women in the story, including Carole herself, whose spoken contributions are significantly minimal. That's a tactful decision on the author's part, and it communicates itself to the actress who becomes both simpler and more affecting as the play's emotions take hold. Naked autobiography in the theatre always seems to me like special pleading, sometimes amounting to emotional blackmail. This production, which I saw at a preview, can't avoid the first charge but keeps honourably clear of the second. - Tijuana Cure is at the Passe Muraille Backspace until March 28. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.
